question: In PHP, `function ship(string $sku) {}` called with `null` throws a `TypeError`. In a C# project with `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>`, `void Ship(string sku)` receives `null` from code that used `!` to silence a warning. What happens when `Ship` is called?
options: The runtime throws `ArgumentNullException` before the method body runs, as PHP throws `TypeError`
The call fails to compile in every caller, because `!` only silences the warning in one place
Nothing at the call; a `NullReferenceException` comes later, at the first dereference
The runtime converts `null` to an empty string, because the parameter is non-nullable
explanation: Nullable reference types are compile-time only, so no runtime check is generated and `null` flows in. The tempting first option describes what you get only if you write `ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(sku)` yourself; PHP's automatic `TypeError` has no C# equivalent for reference types.

question: What is the difference between `int?` and `string?`?
options: `int?` is a runtime `Nullable<int>` struct; `string?` is only a compiler annotation
Both are wrapper types the compiler creates, so both expose `HasValue` and `Value`
Both are annotations only; neither exists at run time, and both compile to the plain type
`string?` makes the string immutable, while `int?` makes the integer optional in method calls
explanation: A nullable value type is a real generic struct, so you can ask `discount.HasValue`. A nullable reference type changes no runtime type at all. Assuming they work the same way leads to looking for a `HasValue` on `string?`, which does not exist.

question: `public class Product { public string Sku { get; set; } }` produces warning CS8618. Every product must have a SKU. Which fix states the design honestly?
options: `public string Sku { get; set; } = null!;`
`public string? Sku { get; set; }`
Add `#nullable disable` at the top of the file
`public required string Sku { get; init; }`
explanation: `required` makes the compiler reject any construction that forgets the SKU, which matches the rule. `= null!` is the tempting quick fix, but it only silences the warning and leaves a real `null` that crashes at run time. `string?` would claim the SKU is optional, which it is not.

question: Inside `if (cache.TryGetValue(sku, out var product)) { product.Name ... }`, why is there no nullability warning on `product`, even though `TryGetValue` must set `product` to a default when the key is missing?
options: `var` infers a non-nullable type for `out` variables, so the analysis skips them
The `out` parameter is declared `[MaybeNullWhen(false)]`, so `true` means not-null
A dictionary with a non-nullable value type can never contain a null value
The compiler reads the body of `TryGetValue` to prove it never returns null
explanation: The attribute encodes "maybe null only when the result is false", and null-state analysis applies it inside the `if`. The analysis never reads into other methods' bodies (the last option), which is exactly why such attributes exist.

question: An API on .NET 10 deserializes `{"Email": null}` into `record Signup(string Email)` with default `System.Text.Json` options. What does `Email` contain?
options: `null`: the serializer ignores nullable annotations by default
An empty string, because the serializer replaces `null` for non-nullable `string` properties
Nothing: deserialization throws `JsonException`, because `Email` is not nullable
The build fails, because the source generator checks the JSON contract against the record
explanation: The serializer ignores nullability annotations unless you set `RespectNullableAnnotations = true` (available since .NET 9); only then does an explicit `null` throw. The third option describes that opt-in behavior, not the default, and even with it a missing property is still not rejected. Nothing checks JSON payloads at build time.

question: Which C# 14 line assigns the address only when `order` is not null, and skips calling `LoadAddress()` otherwise?
options: `order!.ShippingAddress = LoadAddress();`
`order.ShippingAddress ??= LoadAddress();`
`order?.ShippingAddress = LoadAddress();`
`order ?? ShippingAddress = LoadAddress();`
explanation: Null-conditional assignment, new in C# 14, evaluates the right side only when the receiver is not null. `!` merely silences the compiler and throws `NullReferenceException` for a null `order`. `??=` tests the property, not `order`, so it still dereferences a null `order`.
